analysis.one_liner: Exempts on-duty government officials from the federal gun ban for people convicted of domestic violence misdemeanors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee's Crime Subcommittee on July 31, 1997 and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1996, Congress barred anyone convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence from possessing firearms, with no exception for police or other government employees. This bill would have carved government officials back out: while on duty and performing official work for a federal, state, or local government, a person with such a conviction could still possess a firearm. It also would have retroactively wiped out the effect of certain convictions for on-duty conduct committed between the 1996 ban and this bill, treating them as non-convictions under the broader federal gun possession ban. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Government officials — especially law enforcement officers — who have been convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. Under the bill they could keep or carry a firearm while on duty, and some past on-duty convictions would no longer count against them. Government employers and police departments would also be relieved of the dilemma of officers disqualified from carrying weapons by the 1996 law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: On-duty officials with domestic violence convictions

how_it_helps.text: It adds an exemption to federal law so that the ban on gun possession by people convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence (18 U.S.C. 922(g)(9) and 922(d)(9)) does not apply to an official on duty and engaged in official activity of the federal government, a state, or a local government.

It also provides that a conviction for on-duty conduct committed during the period before enactment 'shall not be considered a conviction' for purposes of the separate federal ban on gun possession after certain other convictions — a retroactive protection for officials already caught by the 1996 ban.

analysis.who_pays: Families and partners of government officials, who would remain exposed to an armed abuser while the public faces no such exemption; more broadly, anyone concerned that the same domestic violence conviction would strip an ordinary citizen of gun rights but not an official's. The general public bears the safety risk of convicted domestic abusers carrying firearms on duty.
analysis.who_pays_short: Families of officials with abuse convictions

drawbacks.text: The bill would have allowed a government official with a domestic violence misdemeanor conviction to carry a firearm while on duty, including police officers, leaving the families of officials with less protection from armed abusers than other families.

Section (b) would have retroactively erased the effect of certain convictions for on-duty conduct, treating them as non-convictions for the general ban on gun possession by people with qualifying records — undoing penalties already imposed under the 1996 law.

A fair criticism of the underlying 1996 ban was that it applied to old misdemeanor convictions and could have disarmed police officers hired before the law; a narrow retroactivity fix could have addressed that without a blanket exemption — this bill went well beyond one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There was a real, good-faith concern behind this bill: the 1996 ban applied to misdemeanor convictions, including old ones, and police departments warned it could disarm officers for conduct that predated the law. A narrow fix for that problem could be defended. But this bill was far broader — it created a blanket exemption for any on-duty official and would have retroactively erased convictions for on-duty conduct, leaving the families of government employees, including police officers' families, with less protection than anyone else's. The cost of that unequal treatment outweighed the narrow operational relief it offered.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime Subcommittee, and nobody ever brought it up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: After its introduction and committee referral in July 1997, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime on July 31, 1997, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the 105th Congress.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
Because it never became law, the 1996 domestic violence misdemeanor gun ban continued to apply to government officials the same as to everyone else.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic violence victims and the general public kept the protection of the 1996 federal gun ban intact; no official carve-out was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Domestic violence victims and the general public

for.name: Rep. Gerald Kleczka
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 24, 1997 and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Henry Hyde)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 24, 1997 and sent it to the Subcommittee on Crime, where no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: One Democrat sponsored the bill and no one else, of either party, cosponsored it; no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split shows up in the record.

industries.industry: Government officials and law enforcement officers with domestic violence misdemeanor convictions
industries.note: The bill would have created a special rule for people holding government jobs: a domestic violence conviction would not cost them their firearm while on duty, and on-duty convictions from the 1996-1997 period would have been wiped out retroactively. Ordinary citizens convicted of the same misdemeanor would remain fully barred.
The effect is marginal. The exemption covers possession while on duty, not the general market, so the gun industry would see little direct change.
